newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Serbs set big funeral for slain war-crimes suspect.
newsitem.headline: Serbs set big funeral for slain war-crimes suspect.

text.p: Bosnian Serbs on Friday made elaborate funeral plans for a suspected war criminal killed by NATO in an operation condemned by Russia as a "cowboy raid" which put the peace process at risk.
U.S. President Bill Clinton defended the NATO action, but Washington's fear of retaliation was reflected in a State Department warning to American citizens to take care in Serb-controlled territory.
There was no immediate sign of trouble but a United Nations office in Pale, the stronghold outside Sarajevo of Bosnian Serb nationalists, was the target of a bomb hoax.

British NATO troops on Thursday shot dead Simo Drljaca, the former Serb police chief of the northwestern town of Prijedor, when he resisted arrest, and seized the local hospital director for trial by the U.N. war crimes tribunal. He is now jailed in The Hague.
Authorities in Prijedor, where thousands of Moslems and Croats were "ethnically cleansed" by Drljaca's paramilitary gangs in 1992, said he would be buried on Monday after an autopsy.
He was expected to be interred with full honours with senior political figues in attendance.
His body was returned by peacekeepers, who also released his teenaged son and brother-in-law after detaining them during the shoot-out in which Drljaca died.
A candle-lit vigil in protest against the killing was planned in Prijedor on Friday evening.

The NATO raid implied a switch in tactics by peacekeepers, who have in the past been reluctant to hunt down those on a published list of 67 indicted war criminals, such as former Bosnian Serb President Radovan Karadzic and his army commander General Ratko Mladic.
They and others who believe they might be on a secret list of suspects now fear being grabbed at any time.
Momcilo Krajisnik, a senior Karadzic ally, underlined the concern aroused by the secret indictments at a meeting with international civilian and military representatives.
"We must complain about the existence of some secret, private lists which are causing unease ... there must be no mystery about such lists because that would cause general panic," he told reporters.
A Russian foreign ministry statement said the action in Prijedor went beyond the NATO mandate in Bosnia and hinted Moscow might withdraw its forces from the peacekeeping operation.
"Such cowboy raids threaten the whole Dayton peace process, which is in any case going through a difficult period," it added.
U.N. officials in Sarajevo praised NATO and called for more arrests.
Several British newspapers reported that the operation was carried out by members of the elite Special Air Services (SAS).
Peacekeeping spokesman Chris Riley told reporters on Friday that Drljaca was shot in self-defence when he ignored an order to surrender and drew a pistol, slightly wounding a soldier.
Karadzic lives in the mountain village of Pale, outside Sarajevo, where he is guarded by heavily-armed police and continues to wield power behind the scenes.
Mladic keeps a low profile and was seen this week in the Yugoslav capital Belgrade, where his family lives in an affluent suburb.
